site: Remote worker deployment (scripts/remote/update_worker.sh, run on the Oracle Cloud VM)
class: A deployment script encoded an assumption about how the code reached the machine that did not match how it actually got there, so the one step meant to apply an update failed every time it was run
symptom: Running update_worker.sh against the real Oracle worker to deploy the just-merged f143 fix failed at step [1/4] with 'pkill: killing pid ... Operation not permitted', then at step [2/4] with 'fatal: not a git repository (or any of the parent directories): .git' -- confirmed live, not in a test.
root_cause: update_worker.sh assumed the VM was a git checkout (`git fetch origin && git checkout`) and that the SSH user (`ubuntu`) could signal the daemon directly with `pkill`. Neither was true: /opt/job-automation-agent has no .git directory -- scripts/remote/deploy_to_vm.ps1 (the script that actually provisions and updates this VM) packs the repo on Windows with `tar --exclude=.git` and rsyncs it over, and the daemon runs as systemd user `jobagent` under job-agent-worker.service, not as `ubuntu`, so a bare pkill from ubuntu has no permission to touch it.
why_tests_missed: No test exercised update_worker.sh at all -- there was no regression coverage for scripts/remote/*.sh of any kind, and the script's own failure mode (wrong deployment mechanism assumption) only surfaces when run against a real, already-provisioned VM, which no test in the suite does.
fix: Rewrote update_worker.sh to match the deployment mechanism that is actually in use: it now applies a payload already uploaded to /tmp/jaa.tgz (the same convention deploy_to_vm.ps1 uses) via tar+rsync instead of git, and signals the daemon with `sudo systemctl kill -s SIGTERM job-agent-worker.service` (reaching the jobagent-owned process correctly, and triggering the daemon's own graceful drain handler) instead of pkill. The wait-for-drain step now polls remote_cli.py's worker status instead of a fixed `sleep 5`, matching the script's own stated DRAIN -> WAIT ACTIVE APPLICATION contract.
prevention: A script meant to update or restart a remote machine encodes a claim about how that machine is provisioned (git clone vs. rsync push, which user owns which process) -- that claim is only as good as whoever last provisioned the machine by hand, and drifts silently when the provisioning method changes (here: deploy_to_vm.ps1 replaced the git-based plan this script was written against). When a second script's job is 'update the thing the first script set up,' read the first script before trusting the second one's assumptions, and verify live against the real target at least once rather than only by local review.
